newsitem.title: USA: US holiday sales seen unlikely to trigger Fed move.
newsitem.headline: US holiday sales seen unlikely to trigger Fed move.

text.p: A warmup in U.S. consumer spending during the 1996 holiday shopping season may boost economic growth in the fourth quarter but is unlikely to prompt changes in monetary policy, economists said.
"I don't think holiday sales activity by itself will do anything to the Federal Reserve's policy," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
Wall Street pundits estimate retail sales will rise on average by 4.0 to 6.0 percent between November and December against the same period in 1995.
Although significant, the rise is not considered big enough to push the Federal Reserve to change short-term interest rates one way or another.

"Up four to six percent over a year ago is okay ... But it's not terrific and it certainly will not influence the Federal Reserve," said Irwin Kellner, chief economist at Chase Manhattan's regional bank.
Kellner said such a rise in spending, if confirmed, would not "be a big deal," given the poor retail sales registered late last year due to bad weather, rising layoffs and higher interest rates.

Analysts said the year-end pick-up in demand is not expected to fire up retail inflation, which has held at a remarkably low annual rate of around 2.8 percent for several months now. The absence of inflationary threats will likely prevent the Fed from adjusting rates this year.

"Day after day they (Fed officials) have to pinch themselves to believe that you're getting solid, sustainable economic growth ... with no inflation," said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp.

"In general (the Fed officials') models are telling them that the most likely outcome for the next six to nine months will remain solid growth with relatively low inflation," the chief economist added.
The Fed last changed interest rates in January 1996, when it shaved its target for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to the current 5.25 percent.
Recent statistics show consumers seem willing to empty their wallets with gusto this holiday season.

Same-store sales as measured by TeleCheck, a subsidiary of First Data Corp, rose 4.3 percent in the period between Friday and Sunday after the November 28 Thanksgiving holiday. The data compares to the same period last year.
"Consumers are more confident this year," said William Ford, TeleCheck's senior economic advisor.
The University of Michigan consumer sentiment index jumped to 99.2 in the final November report against 96.5 seen in final October.

The latest report from the Conference Board showed its consumer confidence index remained steady at a strong 107.3 reading in November. The Board said wage gains, low inflation and falling joblessness spell strong holiday sales in 1996.
But one indicator bucked the trend. The closely-watched BTM/Schroders weekly chain store sales index fell 0.2 percent in the week ended November 30 from the prior week.
"I was surprised to see that softness in the BTM index," Daiwa's Moran said.

Yet some analysts said current statistics might be a little bit misleading, since they do not encompass several new methods by which consumers now purchase goods, such as cable television and the Internet.
"Traditional retailers will have competition from another sort this year such as ... home shopping networks and cable as well as your personal computer," Kellner said.

"The consumer's dollar is going to be spread around quite a bit," he said, adding that those purchases were not likely to appear in the current, more conservative statistics which do not include electronic commerce, among other things.
